name: context-provider
intent: Publish a value once at an outer scope so that any descendant subtree can read the nearest published value without every intermediate layer declaring and forwarding it.
problem: Cross-cutting props - theme, locale, current user, feature flags, request/trace context - are owned at an outer node but needed by a sparse set of descendants far below it. Threading them through every intermediate layer produces prop drilling: signatures carry data the component never uses, unrelated layers become coupled to the value, and every new reader forces an edit along the whole path.
context: Tree- or scope-structured programs where an outer node owns a value that a few descendants need and that intermediate nodes must not know about: component trees (React, Compose, SwiftUI, Blazor, Vue), and dynamic scopes such as request contexts, coroutine/task scopes and async-local storage. The value is either read-mostly (theme, locale, session) or scoped to a short-lived execution unit (one request, one task), and the platform or framework is expected to deliver it and to notify or reset readers when the scope ends.
benefits: Readers stop being coupled to the path that leads to them: a new consumer needs one hook/proxy/call instead of a new parameter on every intermediate component or function.
Intermediate layers stay ignorant of the value, so they can be reused in other subtrees and tested without constructing data they do not use.
One place owns the value's lifecycle: the provider or scope manager creates it, publishes it, resets it on exit and (where the framework supports it) notifies readers of changes.
Nested providers give local re-scoping for free: a subtree can override the value - a dark-themed panel, a different account, a test double - without touching the rest of the tree.
Whole-subtree variation becomes cheap: theming, experiment variants and locale switches are applied once at the edge instead of being recomputed per component.
It unlocks framework features that would otherwise need a global variable - routing state, design-system tokens, analytics and trace context - while keeping them tied to a scope that ends.
It enables framework-specific ambient delivery (Flutter's build context, SwiftUI's Environment, Compose's CompositionLocal) that would be impossible with explicit parameters.
Coroutine- and task-scoped values (Python contextvars, AsyncLocal<T>) travel with execution units across async boundaries without manual threading.
tradeoffs: Dependencies become implicit: a reader no longer declares what it needs, so grepping, 'find usages' and stack traces get weaker and debugging usually means walking up the hierarchy to find the nearest provider.

Provider placement is a runtime contract, not a compile-time one: a reader above, beside or outside the provider silently receives the default value (or throws, depending on the ecosystem), and the failure surfaces far from its cause.

Change fan-out is proportional to consumer count: in identity-compared frameworks every consumer re-runs when the published value's identity changes, so unmemoised objects, frequent updates and over-wide providers cost real performance.

Testing and packaging get an extra obligation: every test, story or preview of a consumer must supply a provider, and duplicate copies of the context module (symlinks, duplicated bundles) break the identity match that lookup depends on.

The same API invites drift into global state: used for everything it becomes a service locator or a god context, hiding the dependency graph and re-creating exactly the coupling the pattern was meant to remove.
In React's Strict Mode the provider subtree renders twice in development, which can expose missing memoisation or cause side-effects in setup code that was not designed for double-invocation.
Context key collisions (especially with string keys in large apps) silently resolve to the wrong value; Symbol keys or namespaced string keys are safer but add boilerplate.

participants.responsibility: Identity object that names the value being shared; it holds nothing itself and must be the same object (by identity) for the provider and every reader. Can be a string key, Symbol, class/type reference, or typed token depending on the framework.

Node or scope that publishes a value for the region it encloses; it owns the value's lifetime, its identity and the change notification readers observe. In Vue provide/inject, can be a component or the app-level provider. In Flutter InheritedWidget, the widget itself is the context that broadcasts to descendants.

Descendant that resolves the context to the nearest enclosing published value, reads it without naming the provider, and re-runs or re-renders when that value changes. Must not be the same node as the provider in React (useContext does not see providers rendered by the same component).
Fallback used when no provider encloses the reader; either a legitimate framework default (theme, locale) or an explicit failure signal such as null that a typed accessor rejects.

Nested provider or scope that rebinds the same context for a subset of the tree or for one execution unit, shadowing the outer value until that scope exits. In Python contextvars, this is the token-based reset on context manager exit.

A callback published alongside read-mostly data so that injector components can mutate state through the provider rather than directly, keeping mutation co-located with ownership (used in Vue provide/inject and recommended in React).

use_cases: Theming and appearance: colour scheme, density and elevation tokens published at the app root and read by leaf components (MaterialTheme's CompositionLocals, SwiftUI environment values, ThemeContext provider in React, Vuetify's theme injection).
Identity and session: the currently authenticated user or tenant, with nested providers for 'act as another user' or multi-account surfaces.
Localisation and formatting: locale, time zone and number/date formatters, so leaves format without receiving the locale as a parameter.
Feature flags and experiment variants: a variant assigned once at the edge changes the behaviour of an entire subtree without threading the flag through it.

Request- and task-scoped diagnostics: correlation ids, transaction context and tenant data delivered to every function in a request or task via contextvars (Python), AsyncLocal<T> (.NET), or JavaScript's AsyncContext (proposal).

Component-library configuration: a compound component (select/option, tabs, form fields) publishes its internal parts so children coordinate implicitly instead of receiving coordinated props or cloned elements (Flutter's InheritedModel is purpose-built for this).
Svelte cross-component reactive state: sibling or unrelated components share behaviour through a module-level writable store or context API without a common parent.
Coroutine/task-local resource management: database connections, tracing spans, and feature flags that must follow the async execution flow rather than the call stack.

Cascading values in Blazor: a CascadingValue<T> component wraps a subtree and descendants receive it via [CascadingParameter] matched by type (plus optional Name), so a parent such as a TabSet can cascade itself to its Tab children and coordinate rendering with zero per-child parameter bindings.

Request-scoped execution context in Node.js: AsyncLocalStorage.run(store, callback) binds a request or trace store for one logical operation and getStore() resolves it inside every callback, timer and promise chain the operation spawns - the substrate most Node APM/logging layers use for transaction context.

Provider-scoped services in Angular: a service listed in a component's providers or a route's config creates one instance per subtree, injected by token in descendants; resolution climbs ElementInjectors before falling back to the EnvironmentInjector, giving lazy features and reusable components isolated state per scope.
avoid_when: Only one or two levels separate owner and reader: pass props/parameters - the explicit data flow stays obvious and costs less than a provider.
An intermediate component can render its children as JSX/slots and receive the value itself: extracting that component removes the drilling without hiding the dependency.
The value is local to a subtree that already contains both owner and reader: keep the state where it is used (state colocation) instead of publishing it over a wider scope.

The value is an ordinary service dependency of a handful of modules: constructor/parameter injection keeps the graph explicit and testable, while a context that resolves collaborators is a service locator.

The data changes on every keystroke or frame while many readers observe it: ambient delivery multiplies the update work, so keep hot state local and publish only the minimum that must cross the boundary.

The runtime has no tree or dynamic scope to hang the value on (plain C, most Rust and Go server code): an explicit context object or parameter is more honest than an ambient carrier the language does not provide.
anti_patterns: God context: one provider holding all application state, so every consumer re-runs on every change and the context degenerates into an opaque global store.
Service locator via context: resolving collaborators (database handles, clients, loggers) from the context instead of injecting them, which hides the dependency graph and breaks test isolation.

Consuming your own provider: the reader is the same node that publishes the context (React documents that a component's useContext does not see providers it renders itself), so it silently reads the default or the outer value.
Default value as configuration channel: shipping a production-looking default so a missing provider is never noticed until production or the next refactor moves the provider up the tree.
Unstable published values: providing inline object or function literals, so the value identity changes on every render and every consumer re-runs for nothing.

Vue providing mutable refs without readonly(): injectors that receive a plain reactive ref can mutate the provider's state directly, scattering mutation logic across the tree and breaking the ownership boundary.
Context key name collisions in large apps: using plain string keys across multiple independent features causes silent resolution to the wrong provider when subtrees are composed.

Providing contextvars inside a function or closure: the Context object holds a strong reference to the ContextVar, preventing garbage collection and leaking memory for the lifetime of the context (documented Python pitfall).
design_principles: Inversion of control: the reader asks its scope for the value instead of the owner pushing it through every intermediate signature.
Dependency inversion: readers depend on a stable key or type, not on the concrete component, module or service that supplies the value.
Separation of concerns: value ownership (provider) is separate from value consumption (reader), and intermediate layers keep a single, unrelated responsibility.
Information hiding and least knowledge: the layers in between cannot even name the data they forward, so they cannot accidentally depend on it.
Readmostly-first: prefer publishing immutable or readonly values; treat mutation as a separate concern handled by an explicit updater function published alongside the value.
Narrowest scope: lift the provider only when a second, disjoint subtree genuinely needs the value; prefer props at shallow depths.
best_practices: Keep one context per concern and split read-mostly data from its updater, so changing the updater function does not re-run consumers that only read the data (context splitting pattern).
Publish stable values: hold them in state, memoise objects and callbacks, or freeze them; never construct the published value inline in the provider's render path.

Make absence loud: default to null or a sentinel and let the typed accessor (a useX() hook, a CompositionLocal without default, an environment object read) throw with the provider's name instead of returning a plausible but wrong value.
Place the provider at the narrowest scope that covers all readers and lift it only when a second, disjoint subtree needs the value.
Document the contract next to the accessor: which provider must enclose the reader, what the fallback is, and how to wrap tests, previews and stories.
Refactor in the direction of less scope: once a context has a single reader and a single writer, try props or a plain parameter again before keeping the provider.
In Vue, wrap provided reactive values with readonly() unless injection-side mutation is explicitly intended and documented; prefer the updater-function pattern to keep mutations in the provider.
In Python contextvars, create ContextVar instances at module import time, never inside functions or closures, to avoid memory leaks from Context's strong references.
In Flutter, prefer InheritedModel over InheritedWidget when only a subset of descendants need to react to a change, reducing unnecessary rebuilds.

In SwiftUI, use @Environment rather than ad-hoc @StateObject chains for platform-provided values (scene phase, managed object contexts, presenting a sheet) and reserve environmentObject for app-specific injected services.
Use Symbol injection keys in large Vue/React apps to prevent collisions when multiple features independently define a context with the same string name.
Test readers in isolation by providing a minimal test double context; avoid the temptation to test the reader's behaviour through the real provider in integration tests.
sources: React documentation: Passing Data Deeply with Context - the canonical description of prop drilling, the create/provide/read steps, the use cases and the recommended alternatives (Meta Open Source; context API reshaped with React 16.3, 2018). https://react.dev/learn/passing-data-deeply-with-context
React createContext API reference (Meta Open Source). https://react.dev/reference/react/createContext
React useContext hook reference (Meta Open Source). https://react.dev/reference/react/useContext

Jetpack Compose: Locally scoped data with CompositionLocal - official Android documentation covering creation, providing values, static vs dynamic scoping, and performance characteristics. https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/compositionlocal

Vue Provide / Inject - official Vue.js documentation covering provide/inject with reactive values, readonly(), Symbol keys, app-level provide, injection aliasing, and factory-function default values. https://vuejs.org/guide/components/provide-inject

Python contextvars module - Python Standard Library documentation (added in 3.7, PEP 567), covering ContextVar, Token, copy_context(), Context.run(), and native asyncio support. https://docs.python.org/3/library/contextvars.html

Flutter InheritedWidget class - Flutter/Dart API documentation covering of(), maybeOf(), updateShouldNotify, InheritedModel for partial update notifications, and the context descendant rule. https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/widgets/InheritedWidget-class.html

SwiftUI EnvironmentValues - Apple developer documentation covering environment(_:), environmentObject, @Environment property wrapper, and built-in environment values. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/environmentvalues
Svelte Context API - Simplify State Management article covering get(), set(), and when to use context vs a module-level writable store. https://spin.atomicobject.com

React Context is Dependency Injection, Not State Management - Test Double blog post arguing for restricting Context to DI use cases and criticising its use for high-frequency state updates. https://testdouble.com
React Context Performance Pitfalls - discussion of unnecessary re-renders, context splitting strategies, memoisation requirements, and Strict Mode double-invocation issues. https://blog.devgenius.io

ASP.NET Core Blazor cascading values and parameters - official Microsoft documentation covering CascadingValue<T> subtree broadcasting, [CascadingParameter] resolution by type and Name, root-level values via AddCascadingValue, isFixed/NotifyChangedAsync update subscriptions, and the TabSet cascades-itself coordination pattern. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/blazor/components/cascading-values-and-parameters?view=aspnetcore-10.0

Node.js documentation: Asynchronous context tracking (AsyncLocalStorage) - official docs covering run(store, callback), getStore(), exit(), snapshot(), and the guidance to prefer run() over enterWith() because enterWith() can leak context into the caller's synchronous execution. https://nodejs.org/api/async_context.html

Angular guide: Hierarchical injectors - official documentation covering EnvironmentInjector, ModuleInjector and ElementInjector, climb-the-tree resolution rules, skipSelf/host modifiers, and how providers declared on components or routes scope instances to a subtree. https://angular.dev/guide/di/hierarchical-dependency-injection

React State Management in 2025 (DeveloperWay) - criticism of defaulting to Context for shared state: 'Providers Hell' of nested providers with implicit dependencies, every consumer re-rendering on any change to a merged context, and guidance to split providers or move to dedicated stores. https://www.developerway.com/posts/react-state-management-2025

Common React Context Mistakes: Performance Guide and Best Practices (VOID) - catalogs the catch-all god context, high-frequency data in context, inline object/function literals that break identity, and mixing state with actions; prescribes split API/state contexts and memoisation. https://void.ma/en/publications/react-context-erreurs-performances/
